summary: Buffalo's octagonal limestone tower at the Buffalo River mouth: first lit 1818, the 1833 tower dark as an aid since 1914, now open on tour days.

lens.where: acrylic replica in the lantern since 2015; the four-panel third-order lens from 1905 is on display at the Buffalo and Erie County Historical Society

structures.note: Octagonal cut-limestone tower on a stone molehead (USLHS: limestone and cast iron). Height disputed: 44 ft to the lantern in 1833 (Penberthy); 68 ft after the 1856 rework (Penberthy); 61.5 ft base to lantern centre (USLHS). Cited 1, 2, 3.
New keepers' residence built in 1899 (Penberthy). The earlier dwelling stood beside the original 1818 light (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record lists no keepers' quarters. Cited 1, 2, 3.

staffing.note: Discontinued in 1914; the roster's last principal keeper is John Safe (1905-1914).

access.note: On Coast Guard property. Grounds open during daylight in season; the tower opens on scheduled tour days or by appointment; groups of 30 or more need a reservation (Step Out Buffalo, citing the association).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner); Buffalo Lighthouse Association (leased since 1984, manages the tower)

events.note: Oliver Forward, collector of the port, buys the site at the mouth of Buffalo Creek for $351.50 of his own money (Penberthy)
Station's first light, a 30-foot stone tower (Penberthy) or a sloping conical tower built in 221 days (LighthouseFriends); Putnam dates the first lights to 1818
Steamboat Walk-in-the-Water driven onto the beach near the light in a storm on 31 October 1821; LighthouseFriends says the lighthouse served as a rescue station
Treasury Department appropriates $2,500 to build a pier, lighthouse and ice-breaker; Penberthy gives completion by 15 November 1829, LighthouseFriends 1828
Octagonal cut-limestone tower completed, the year cut in the lintel; USLHS gives 1833 as the year the tower was established
Greenish lens removed after tests showed the reflectors alone gave a better light (Penberthy)
Great Storm of 1844: lake water pushed into Buffalo; breaches in the breakwater toward the light; stones of up to two tons moved more than twenty feet
Lighthouse Board nominates the tower for a third-order Fresnel lens and sets aside $2,500 for a fog bell
Third-order Fresnel lens installed after the tower and lantern were reworked (68 ft by Penberthy's count; focal plane 76 ft per LighthouseFriends). USLHS gives 1857 for the original lens
Appropriation of $30,000 for two lighthouses at the breakwater (Penberthy)
Breakwater north-end light completed; the fog bell from the 1833 tower moved to it (Penberthy)
A vessel's anchor tore up the pipe that supplied the station with water from the river (Light-House Board report)
Lighthouse Board votes to change the characteristic from a fixed glow to white flashes
Four-panel third-order lens by Chance Brothers & Co. installed 8 April 1905, flashing white every five seconds; cost $3,386.74
Two-ton coal bin built into the tower's lower level after a keeper complained about the watchroom heat
Discontinued; USLHS gives 1914 as the year discontinued
Four-panel lens relocated to a new breakwater lighthouse
Red occulting light on a steel skeletal tower set up on the south pier, just east of the old light
Restoration after the 1950s plan to demolish the tower for river widening was halted by public outcry
Briefly relit with floodlights for the bicentennial
Briefly relit with floodlights for Buffalo's sesquicentennial
NPGallery record gives 19 July 1984 as its date published; LighthouseFriends gives 1979. The record's PDF is 22 KB, so the nomination text could not confirm the date
Tower leased by the Coast Guard to the Buffalo Lighthouse Association (association's own site: formed 1985)
Fourth-order bivalve lens from the South Buffalo light displayed in the lantern until 2013
Coast Guard announces it will relinquish a few of its 31 acres on the point; Congressman Brian Higgins obtains over $6 million for public access
Lighthouse opened to the public in October 2011
Fourth-order lens taken down for repair; later restored and displayed at the Heritage Discovery Center
Acrylic third-order replica lens installed in the lantern on 28 September 2015
Relit with the acrylic replica lens on 25 June 2016; not an official aid to navigation

corrections.why: The USLHS record gives a light height of 76 feet above water (about 23.2 m). The 7.6 m figure looks like 76 feet read as metres.

LighthouseFriends describes a white flash every five seconds from the 1905 lens, which served until the light was discontinued in 1914. No source here gives a red occulting characteristic for the Main light. Only a record of the south-pier red light would give Oc R.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends gives the National Register listing as 1979. The NPGallery record (NRIS 84002383) gives 'Date Published' 19 July 1984, which is not the same thing as a listing date, and its PDF is 22 KB, apparently a placeholder. The story gives both dates with their sources and does not settle the question.
The record's 1833 first-lit date belongs to the octagonal tower built in 1833. The station's first light dates from 1818 (Putnam; LighthouseFriends; Penberthy).

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on several dates and heights, and the story states each disagreement: the first lit date (1818 against 1833 in the record), the 1856 lens date (LighthouseFriends, Penberthy) against 1857 (USLHS), the tower height (44 ft in 1833, 68 ft after 1856 per Penberthy; 61.5 ft base to lantern centre per USLHS), the 1826 contract deadline (1829 Penberthy; 1828 LighthouseFriends), and the early keeper dates (LighthouseFriends against USLHS for Jones, Russell, Ramsdell). The story follows the USLHS roster dates. LighthouseFriends alone names John E. Skaats (1818-1827) and James Anderson (1855-1859); they are marked as LighthouseFriends-only. The roster lines are copied as printed by roster.py, which matched the station by name and position (0.04 km). The 1837 Pendergast quotation is from the Navy's own report, as LighthouseFriends quotes it; the primary report was not read. Walk-in-the-Water (1821), the 1905 lens cost, the 1906 coal bin, the 1950s demolition plan, and the 1962 restoration rest on LighthouseFriends alone. Penberthy's article is read through the Buffalo Architecture and History excerpt. The NRHP nomination is not digitised on NPGallery (the 22 KB placeholder), and HABS NY-60 was not readable (loc.gov returned 403 and the USLHS copy has no text layer), so no architectural record was consulted. Newspaper searches on Chronicling America for the keepers returned no usable pages, and the 1872 Chicago Tribune item that turned up is a feature about a different keeper and was not used. The 1914 discontinuance is supported by the USLHS record and LighthouseFriends; no official report was found to confirm it. The 'Chinaman's Light' nickname LighthouseFriends mentions for a later wooden tower was left out as unsourced context. Wikipedia was used only for leads and is not cited. Current visiting terms come from Step Out Buffalo's listing; check the association's site before publishing. Corpus greps for the Commissioner and Bulletin years found no official entry for the Main light's 1914 discontinuance; the Bulletin's 1914 entries concern the new breakwater light. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the story now states the disagreements on the breakwater length (LighthouseFriends 2,500 ft against Penberthy 4,000 ft), on the NRHP date (NPGallery 'Date Published' 19 July 1984 against LighthouseFriends 1979) and on current visiting status (LighthouseFriends 'Grounds open seasonally, tower closed' against the Step Out Buffalo tour listing). The 1892 and 1894 Light-House Board entries are dated to their fiscal years (1891-92, 1893-94). The 1906 coal bin, 1905 lens cost and 1821 Walk-in-the-Water items rest on LighthouseFriends alone and are sourced as such. Footnote 6 is checked against the scan page (corpus.py page general 1917: scan p.205). Footnotes 7 and 8 are checked against entries 1088 and 1080 (scan pp.187 and 501). Step Out Buffalo's listing does not name the Buffalo Lighthouse Association; the footnote now describes what the listing says. Roster lines are copied from the USLHS page (src3), which prints its headings as 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper', '1st Assistant Lighthouse Keeper' and 'Contractor'.
